prompt:
Passage:
The Blurred Photograph

Sofia had taken 312 photographs at the Riverside Market, and she trusted exactly eight of them. Those eight showed straight rows of oranges, shining jars of honey, and vendors standing sharply inside the rectangles of their stalls. She printed them for the school exhibit called “Saturday in Our Neighborhood” and arranged them across her bedroom floor.

Her younger cousin Luis leaned over the doorway. “Where’s mine?”

Sofia knew which picture he meant. She had let him use her camera for one minute while she tied her shoe. He had pressed the button as a baker passed a loaf to a small child. The child’s red sleeve swept across the image, the baker’s hands were doubled by motion, and the background tilted. Sofia had saved the photograph only because deleting someone else’s work felt rude.

“It’s blurry,” she said.

“They were moving,” Luis replied, as if that explained everything.

At school, Ms. Nwosu, the exhibit adviser, helped Sofia hang the eight prints. She stepped back, then walked from one end of the wall to the other. “Beautiful control,” she said. “What did the market sound like?”

Sofia waited for a comment about lighting or balance. “Sound like?”

“These pictures make me feel that everyone held still until you left.”

The remark followed Sofia home. She opened the folder containing the other 304 photographs. Most deserved to stay there: closed eyes, blocked faces, a finger in front of the lens. Then she reached Luis’s picture. The baker’s moving hands formed a pale arc around the loaf. The child’s sleeve seemed to pull the eye toward it. Sofia could almost hear the paper bag crackle.

The next morning, she printed the photograph. On paper, the blur was even more obvious. She carried it to the market and showed it to Mr. Rami, the baker.

“That’s Anika,” he said, recognizing the child. “She saves coins all week for our Saturday bread.” He did not complain about his doubled hands. Instead, he traced the pale arc without touching the paper. “That is exactly how busy it gets.”

Sofia returned to the exhibit wall and moved two of her stillest photographs apart. She placed Luis’s image between them. At first, it looked like a mistake interrupting a careful sentence. Then the neighboring pictures changed. The neat row of bread on one side seemed ready to be lifted; the empty basket on the other looked recently emptied.

At the exhibit opening, visitors paused longest near the blurred photograph. Luis arrived and read the small label beneath it: “Bread Exchange, photograph by Luis Moreno.”

“You used mine,” he said.

Sofia studied the wall. She still loved the clean lines in her eight photographs. But now they had somewhere to go. “It made the others move,” she said.

Question:
Why has Sofia kept Luis’s photograph even though she does not initially plan to display it?

choices.A: Ms. Nwosu has already selected it for the exhibit.
choices.B: Deleting another person’s photograph feels rude to her.
choices.C: Mr. Rami has asked to purchase it.
choices.D: It is the only image she took at the market.

explanation: The passage states that Sofia saved the blurred photograph only because deleting someone else’s work felt rude.

prompt:
Passage:
Passage A: A New Score for an Old Screen

When I accompany a silent film on piano, I am not trying to hide the film’s age. I am helping a present-day audience enter its rhythm. A chase may need a quick pulse, while a long glance between characters may be stronger with only a few quiet notes. The film guides me, but no single melody is required by every image.

New music can reveal connections that an older score did not emphasize. A repeated theme might link two characters who rarely share the screen. An unusual instrument might draw attention to the machines in a film about city life. Different musicians can make different choices while still respecting the same work.

Improvisation does not mean arriving unprepared. I watch the film repeatedly, mark important changes, and research the setting. Programs should identify the composer and date of any new score so audiences do not mistake it for original music. A thoughtful modern accompaniment is not a replacement for history. It is one more documented conversation with the film.

Passage B: Listen for the Evidence

Many silent films were never truly silent. Theaters employed pianists or small ensembles, and distributors sometimes supplied cue sheets suggesting particular kinds of music for individual scenes. Surviving scores, cue sheets, and theater records can reveal how early audiences may have experienced a film.

Before creating new accompaniment, musicians should examine that evidence. A historical cue may explain why a scene changes mood suddenly or why an apparently minor character receives a musical theme. Following an old score can also restore contrasts that a modern viewer might otherwise overlook.

Historical evidence is often incomplete. A cue sheet may be missing pages, and two theaters may have played different music for the same film. In such cases, modern choices are unavoidable. Those choices should be made visible rather than presented as recovered fact. Performances might use surviving music where possible and newly composed passages where necessary. The goal is not to freeze every screening into one form, but to let evidence participate in the performance.

Question:
Which choice best states the central idea of Passage A?

choices.A: Silent films should be shown without any musical accompaniment.
choices.B: Every silent film has one required melody that all musicians must use.
choices.C: A prepared and clearly identified modern score can offer a respectful new interpretation of an older film.
choices.D: Musicians should improvise without watching or researching the film first.

explanation: Passage A supports new musical choices guided by repeated viewing and research, provided programs identify the score as a modern interpretation.

prompt:
Passage:
Finding the Way Back

Digital directions often tell travelers exactly when to turn. Such instructions can make a first trip efficient, but cognitive researcher Imani Wells wondered whether they help people remember a route afterward. Her team compared turn-by-turn directions with prompts that called attention to landmarks.

Eighty students who had never visited a large botanical garden participated. Each student followed the same winding path from the entrance to a greenhouse. Half received arrow instructions on a handheld device, such as “Turn left in 40 meters.” The other half received landmark prompts, such as “At the stone fountain, turn toward the bamboo gate.” Both devices displayed one instruction at a time and gave no overhead map.

On the first trip, researchers measured travel time and wrong turns. After a twenty-minute activity inside the greenhouse, the devices were collected. Students were then asked to walk the route in reverse without assistance. At the end, they sketched the route and marked any features they remembered.

During the guided trip, the arrow group arrived about two minutes sooner on average and made slightly fewer wrong turns. On the return trip, however, the landmark group made 35 percent fewer wrong turns than the arrow group. Their sketches also placed more turns in the correct relation to one another and included more accurate features from the garden.

Interviews suggested a possible explanation. Several arrow-group students said they watched the distance counter and waited for the next command. Landmark-group students described searching ahead for fountains, gates, and unusual trees. One student said, “I had to match the words to a real place, so the turn had a reason to stick.”

The study does not prove that landmark prompts are always superior. The participants walked one route in good weather, and they knew they were part of a study. A busy street, a nighttime trip, or a traveler carrying heavy bags might produce different results. Also, the arrow group’s faster first trip could matter when speed is the main goal.

Wells argues that route instructions serve at least two purposes: guiding a person now and helping that person learn the surroundings. The best design may depend on which purpose matters more. A system could even combine methods, supplying precise distance information while naming stable features worth noticing.

prompt:
Passage:
A Spinning Seed’s Balance

Some trees release seeds attached to a thin wing. As the seed falls, the wing may rotate, slowing the descent and giving wind more time to carry the seed away from the parent tree. Engineer Pavel Arun wondered how the location of weight along the wing affects this spinning motion.

Arun’s team built ninety artificial seeds from identical paper wings and tiny metal beads. In one group, the bead sat near the thick base where a natural seed body would be. In a second group, the bead sat halfway along the wing. In a third, it sat near the wing tip. Every model had the same total mass, wing area, and overall length.

The researchers released each model from the top of a six-meter indoor chamber. Still air prevented unpredictable gusts. High-speed cameras recorded when the model began to rotate, how steadily it spun, and how many seconds it took to reach a padded floor.

Base-weighted models began rotating after the shortest drop and followed the steadiest paths. They also had the longest average descent time. Middle-weighted models usually rotated, but many rocked from side to side before settling into a regular spin. Tip-weighted models often tumbled or slid sideways, reaching the floor sooner.

To understand the pattern, the team measured each model’s center of mass—the point around which its weight was balanced. With weight near the base, the heavy end tended to lead downward while the broad paper wing met the air above it. This arrangement made a stable rotation easier to establish. Moving weight toward the tip shifted the balance and made the model more likely to wobble.

The team then tested natural seeds from three tree species. All carried most of their mass close to one end of the wing, and many showed the same early, steady rotation as the base-weighted models. The natural seeds differed in shape and stiffness, however, so their descent times could not be compared directly with those of the paper models.

An indoor drop chamber simplifies the conditions a seed meets outdoors. Wind can lift, push, or interrupt a spinning seed, and rain can change a wing’s mass and flexibility. The artificial models also lacked veins and curved surfaces. Even so, holding most features constant allowed the experiment to isolate one important factor: where a winged seed carries its weight.

Question:
Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Wing area is the only feature that determines how a seed falls.
choices.B: Tip-weighted seeds remain in the air longer because they tumble.
choices.C: Keeping weight near the base of a wing can help a falling seed establish stable rotation and descend more slowly.
choices.D: Natural seeds carry equal amounts of weight at every point along their wings.

explanation: Base-weighted models started rotating sooner, followed steadier paths, and had longer descent times; natural seeds also concentrated mass near one end.

An indoor drop chamber simplifies the conditions a seed meets outdoors. Wind can lift, push, or interrupt a spinning seed, and rain can change a wing’s mass and flexibility. The artificial models also lacked veins and curved surfaces. Even so, holding most features constant allowed the experiment to isolate one important factor: where a winged seed carries its weight.

Question:
Which choice best summarizes the experiment’s findings?

choices.A: All weight locations produced identical rotation because the models had equal mass.
choices.B: Middle-weighted models never rotated, while tip-weighted models remained aloft longest.
choices.C: Base-weighted models rotated earlier and more steadily and descended longer, a pattern also observed in many natural seeds despite other differences.
choices.D: Natural seeds carried most of their mass at the wing tip and could be compared directly with paper models.

explanation: Base-weighted models performed best for early stable rotation and slow descent, and natural seeds with mass near one end often showed similar rotation, though their shapes differed.
